title: Mab Ashby's Bee-Book
author: the Ashbys of the bee-tree
body:
# The Bee-Tree

*A keeper's book, in pencil, the early pages in three different hands and the last forty in one.*

---

Twelve hives in the tree and four on the bench. Swarmed off the north limb at Whitsun, took it in the Tamwick fingerpost, hived it in the low log. Wax to the Moot, nine pound.

The tree's dead and the bees don't care. Gran said it was the bees killed it, wanting it hollow, and she said it the way you'd say the bees were right.

*The last page, in a bigger and less steady hand:*

Linnet. When it's me, you tell them. Knock three times on the low log and say it plain, my name and that I'm dead and that you keep them now. Don't dress it. They know when you dress it. Then tie the black on, if you haven't, and leave them a comb's worth of the honey, and they'll stay.

If you can't say it, get somebody to stand with you that can. That's allowed. Gran had the verderer.

title: The Mote's Customs
author: cut on the board by the dog-gauge
body:
# Customs of the Swainmote

*Cut into an oak board on two posts beside the gauge, the letters filled with tar that has mostly gone.*

---

Twelve sit. Who comes into the ring while the mote is short may sit, and is a Woodman for the day.

The steward says custom. He does not make it.

A hound that passes the stirrup is a hound. A hound that does not is a danger to the harts, and is lawed: three claws from each forefoot, and no more.

What is taken from a living tree, the tree must spare.

What is given back is not counted against the one who took.

What the mote witnesses, the mote remembers.

*Under it, newer, cut with a knife:* The knights' oaths are in the steward's roll. Ask.

title: Laithe's Rule
author: Margery Laithe
body:
# The Walk's Rule

*Cut on a board nailed to the jack's frame, at a ropewalker's eye height, which is low.*

---

Three into yarn, sunwise.
Three yarn into strand, widdershins.
Three strand into line, sunwise again.
What is laid against itself holds.

Walk backward. Never turn your back on the jack.

Good silk sings in the wind on the posts. Silk that does not sing has been where it should not have been. Do not lay it.

*Below, in chalk, fresh:* Black silk in from the south again. Will not sing. Will not lay. Where are the Dunnocks.

title: Gammer Hoole's Count
author: Gammer Hoole
body:
# The Count

*A hazel stick notched on three sides, a notch a call, and wrapped round it a paper in a careful, unpractised hand.*

---

The owl calls at the top of the sun. Count. Do not look up, it does not like to be looked at.

One call is nothing lost.
Three is a thing dropped on a road.
Five is a thing under the ground.
Seven is a thing somebody hid.
Nine is a place.

It called nine at the Long Wind and the next morning the Brother was down and the dark under him open. It called nine yesterday.

*On the stick's third side, newer than the rest, nine notches in a row.*

title: A Gall-Wright's Day-Book
author: Orrin Sable, wright to the Sayers' Circle
body:
# Day-Book of the Knar Works

*A Lantern Row ledger, its pages gone stiff and grey with ink-fume. The hand gets smaller as it goes.*

---

**First year.** Twelve barrels to the Circle. The black is all they said. Wrote my name on a board in it and put the board in the river a week, and it came up as I wrote it.

**Third year.** Eighteen barrels. The cutters will not sleep in the gall; they say it is listening. Told them to drink a little of the black at night, which is what the Woodfolk would call taking more than you need. It works. Nobody sleeps.

**Sixth year.** Twenty-six barrels. The crown is going grey on the north side. The Circle wants thirty.

**Ninth year.** Took on two silk-gatherers from the north who came asking for work, a brother and sister, for the gall-silk on the bores. The brother says he wants to go home. Nobody goes home. The Circle wants thirty.

*The last entry is a single line, in a hand so small it is almost a row of dots:* Could not remember my name this morning. Looked it up. It is written here in the black, so it is kept.

title: A Letter under the Circle's Seal
author: the Clerk of the Rolls, Tollmere
body:
# To Master Sable, at the Works

*Folded small and pushed under a cutter's bedding, the seal broken. It was read many times.*

---

Master Sable,

The Circle thanks you for the twenty-sixth barrel and asks for thirty. The Rolls of the Unsaid grow faster than the Rolls of the Said this year, and both want the black. A name struck from the Rolls must be struck in the same ink it was written in, or it is not struck, and the Circle does not do things that are not done.

As to the tree, the Circle does not hold with the Woodfolk's custom of sparing, which is a custom for those who have no records. When the tree is done, the Circle will find another.

The Clerk of the Rolls
